Oil News: Ceasefire Hopes Test Crude as Hormuz Risk Keeps Brent Supported
Proposed Russian diesel shipments and ceasefire hopes eased immediate supply pressure, pushing gasoil futures down 3%.
Ukraine is still awaiting ceasefire details and Russia has not commented, leaving the energy deal unverified.
Hormuz tanker attacks, Saudi strikes and Gulf production restarts pull the crude supply outlook in opposite directions.
Peace Headlines Test Crude as Hormuz Risk Holds the Floor
Crude starts the week caught between two stories that do not cancel each other out. The Russia-Ukraine ceasefire and a promise of Russian diesel gave sellers a headline to work with Monday. The Strait of Hormuz attacks and the Saudi airport strikes were not part of any deal.
Sellers have the diplomatic angle, but confirmed barrels and safe shipping lanes are still missing from the trade.
December WTI crude oil futures finished 1.34% higher last week. Brent held above $100 per barrel despite the latest push to ease refined-product tightness.
Next up Natural Gas and Oil Forecast: WTI Tests $91.40, Can Brent Break $106 and NG Reach $3.35?
Weekly December WTI Crude Oil Futures Technical Analysis
December WTI crude oil futures opened the week under pressure early Monday after finishing 1.34% higher last week. The main trend is up according to the weekly swing chart. A trade through $96.41 will signal a resumption of the uptrend. The main trend will change to down on a break through $71.00.
The minor trend is up. A trade through last week’s high at $92.14 will turn $86.00 into a new minor bottom.
The minor range is $96.41 to $86.00. Its pivot at $91.21 is likely to control the direction of the market this week.
The nearest support is a pair of 50% levels at $83.71 to $81.69. With the main trend up, buyers could show up on a pullback into this area. A failure to hold $81.69 could trigger an acceleration to the downside with $76.02 to $71.21 the next major target zone. Inside this zone is the 52-week moving average at $71.95. This indicator has been controlling the trend since late January.
Every new Brent Oil analysis as it publishes, today's technical signal and key levels, live price — on one page.
Weekly December Brent Crude Oil Futures Technical Analysis
December Brent crude oil futures are lower early Monday. The market is trading inside last week’s range, suggesting trader indecision. The main trend is up according to the weekly swing chart. A trade through $105.92 will signal a resumption of the uptrend. The main trend will change to down on a trade through $75.77.
The minor trend is also up. A trade through $93.68 will change the minor trend to down and shift momentum to the downside.
A trade through $105.92 will put $113.14 on the radar. On the downside, the first pivot price to watch is $99.80. This pivot is likely to control the direction of the market this week. Buyers could step in on a pullback into this level, but if it fails as support, Brent futures will be vulnerable to a correction into the main trend 50% level at $94.41 and the minor swing bottom at $93.68.
Russian Diesel Deal Takes Some Heat Out of the Trade
Trump announced Russian diesel headed for global markets. More than 300,000 metric tons immediately, another 500,000 metric tons in November, and 1 million metric tons after that. Gasoil futures dropped 3% to $1,436 per barrel on the news.
Global diesel consumption runs near 29 million barrels per day, so the announced volumes ease some of the tightness without rebalancing the market on their own. Additionally, the International Energy Agency is pressing members to assess whether additional diesel releases are needed and to accelerate pledged volumes that have not been delivered.
The ceasefire is the same trade. Trump said both sides agreed to stop hitting energy facilities. Ukraine said it was waiting for details. Russia did not comment.
Hormuz and Saudi Attacks Keep the Supply Risk Alive
T he Middle East risk has not gone away. The Houthis claimed responsibility for a strike on Riyadh’s international airport Saturday. Saudi authorities reported another attack on the airport Sunday. Trump said the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis.
The shipping story is just as important. United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported that one tanker was struck by a drone near Sohar anchorage in Oman and another was damaged moving through the Strait of Hormuz. More attacks this month threaten the recovery in Middle East crude exports seen in September.
None of that changed with the ceasefire discussion. A Russia-Ukraine deal on energy facilities does not extend to the Red Sea or the Gulf shipping lanes.
Shell, Chevron and BP were redeploying personnel after Hurricane Isaias made landfall Saturday. Gulf of Mexico production coming back takes away the supply story that helped WTI late last week. That puts more near-term pressure on the WTI side of the market.
Goldman Sachs said high U.S.-Europe shipping costs have widened the WTI-Brent spread. Goldman raised its December Brent forecast to $90 per barrel from $85 and estimated the geopolitical risk premium at just over $20 per barrel. The bank forecast WTI at $81 in December 2026 and $73 in 2027.
The ceasefire has not been verified and the diesel has not been loaded, but Gulf production restarts are already adding supply back into the market. On the other side, the Hormuz shipping risk and Saudi airport attacks are not part of any negotiation. Sellers had the diplomatic headline Monday. The tanker attacks near Hormuz kept them from finishing the job.
WTI’s pivot at $91.21 controls the week. Buyers are taking offers above that level. The next support sits at $83.71 to $81.69.
Brent held above $100 with $99.80 underneath as the floor for the risk premium trade. The Hormuz premium and the wider WTI spread are both in the price.

The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, has said Russia rejects the idea of a temporary ceasefire, telling reporters that Moscow wanted a long-term peace deal instead.
“In the Kremlin, both ‌President Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated that ​we do not want a ceasefire,” said Peskov. “We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible ⁠to achieve it.“
Peskov’s comments were a rejection of a ⁠60-day ceasefire idea proposed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ⁠on Sunday to allow ⁠his ​country to hold presidential elections. Kyiv has accused Russia of violating temporary truces when ceasefires between the two sides have been agreed to in the past.
Peskov was asked to comment on Trump’s self-declared “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine and refused to be drawn on it, only saying:
Contacts continue. As soon as we have something to say on the matter, we will inform you.

Ukrainian officials said Russian attacks killed six people in two Ukrainian cities yesterday.
In Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, a strike on a grocery store killed three people and injured 20 others, including two children, the regional governor, Oleh Syniehubov, said.
Footage released by the Kharkiv prosecutor’s office captured the moment of the strike, showing debris flying through the air and fires breaking out as car alarms sounded.

An “unprecedented” cyber-attack is behind the shutdown of refrigerator units in multiple French supermarkets, according to the chief executive of Cooperative U, one of the chains affected.
At least 150 Intermarche shops were targeted, along with almost 100 Cooperative U outlets, AFP reports. Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, with media reporting that hackers were “managing to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores.”
Reuters is carrying some further quotes from Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe , Gen Alexus Grynkewich , about how the alliance says it would deal with an attack on Nato territory. He told the audience at the Warsaw Security Forum:
If someone ​is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight. We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be. We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, ⁠proves utterly futile.
Should the adversary ​choose to press ‌the attack ​or commit his reserves, ​we will break the warfighting system engaged against us. This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force.
The US general is speaking just days after president Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel .
Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe , Gen Alexus Grynkewich has been outlining what he describes as the Nato “theory of victory”, in which he says Nato forces would block, then blunt, then break any aggressive move against the alliance.
While stressing that he did not see conflict as “inevitable”, he said at the Warsaw Security Forum it was a plan to “prepare us to execute our most sacred task – the defence of our people and our territory.”
Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe , Gen Alexus Grynkewich , is speaking now at the Warsaw Security Forum. We will bring you any key lines that emerge.

A little more from Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov here on the prospects of a limited truce agreement. He says that Russia would potentially offer a one-day truce if Ukraine were to hold elections. He said:
If they truly want to hold elections in Kyiv, then the president of Russia, the commander-in-chief, will be ready to give an order not to launch strikes on Ukraine on election day, specifically on election day.
France’s high school students will stage new protests on Tuesday, the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency is reporting,
A government source told journalists last week that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations, which have shaken an unpopular government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit, was already “at least 30 million euros”.
Widespread disillusionment has seen young people protest over recent weeks against what they say is underfunding and neglect of the education system, with the demonstrations marred by often violent clashes that have injured hundreds.
Trying to appease the student’s demands, the government announced last week that about 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
But the Union of High School students described the initial announcements as “crumbs” and maintain their demand for an extra €10m (£8.4m) to be invested in the country’s lycees, where students – most between 15 and 18 – complete their high school education.
On Friday, the government noted a drop in the number of blockades and meetings outside the country’s lycees. More than 96% were opening on Friday, the education ministry said, but now a new stage of the campaign for improved conditions could mark a turning point in the protests.
Protesters and high-school students take part in a demonstration outside the Lycee Toulouse Lautrec, in Toulouse on 12 OCtober 2026. Photograph: Ed Jones/AFP/Getty Images The EU has added almost 1,600 new individuals and entities to its sanctions blacklist over Russia’s war on Ukraine .
“This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said. She added:
Europe is again showing a united front. More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles.
We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians.
The European lawmaker Raphaël Glucksmann has urged the French centre left to wage an “existential battle” to prevent Marine Le Pen ’s far right winning the 2027 presidential election after he was chosen as the social democrat candidate for the presidency.
“We’ve got to rid our hearts of the spirit of defeat,” Glucksmann, the founder of the small party Place Publique, said on Monday morning after his decisive win in a centre-left primary race held by the Socialist party.
In his first interview since being designated a presidential candidate on Sunday night, Glucksmann told France Inter radio that the country was living in a “historic moment”, with the far right at the gates of power. He said the 2027 presidential election campaign would be brutal and “like no other we have ever experienced”. He said it would be unbearable to have a centre left “that doesn’t believe in victory”, adding that he could restore a “pride in social democracy”.
At present the centre left sits substantially behind the far right in the polls and also trails the radical left politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon , who is polling high but with whom Glucksmann refuses to work. You can read more here:
French centre left must wage ‘existential battle’ to prevent far right winning presidency

“In the Kremlin, both ‌President Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated that ​we do not want a ceasefire,” said Peskov. “We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible ⁠to achieve it.“
Peskov’s comments were a rejection of a ⁠60-day ceasefire idea proposed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ⁠on Sunday to allow ⁠his ​country to hold presidential elections. Contacts continue. As soon as we have something to say on the matter, we will inform you.
In other news, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government came under renewed pressure this morning after a key minister from its junior coalition partner, the SPD, unexpectedly quit.
Baerbel Bas, labour minister and co-leader of the centre-left SPD, cited personal reasons for her resignation, saying she needed time to grieve after the death of her stepdaughter.
But she also criticised Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which is in crisis after heavy recent electoral defeats, notably the far-right AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt last month .
“I must unfortunately note that the public attacks against me – regrettably including those from within the ranks of our coalition partner – have continued to intensify during this difficult time for me personally,” Bas said. She will reportedly replaced as labour minister by Alexander Schweitzer, one of the SPD’s vice-chairs.
The resignation comes amid turmoil for the government, which is grappling with a sluggish economy and low poll ratings.
Bas intends to retain her seat as an MP for Duisburg, a city at the heart of the former Ruhr mining region in northern Germany. Photograph: Maryam Majd/Reuters The Nobel Prize for economics has been awarded to Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford, for their work on the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”.
[Reminder: As we flagged earlier , Woodford was among the predicted winners – he’s one of the architects of modern forward guidance, the idea that central banks can control the economy through influencing public expectations about inflation, rather than just through interest rates.]
The S veriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel is worth 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000), plus the glory of course, and the knowledge that every pronouncement you make now comes with the authority of a Nobel Prize winner.

Zelenskyy said Trump’s energy ceasefire announcement caught him by surprise, first hearing about it through the media.
No, we did not know about that. We’ve learned that from the media as well that the president of the United States has secured an energy ceasefire.
I thought perhaps their team reached out to the Russians. I think they are in constant contact in a certain format.
During a Q&A with journalists, Zelenskyy said he’s ready to find ways to alter the constitution to be able to hold elections “very quickly” if a “full” energy ceasefire is implemented. He said this may require “difficult (legislative) solutions”.
“As of now, it is very difficult because of the security level in our cities and villages and communities. It is also impossible now because of our military. More than a million people who must vote – but how will they vote while being on the frontline?”
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the country has been under martial law, meaning elections are suspended.
But Donald Trump , under pressure ahead of the November elections, said on Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the US, even though they have largely been affected by his war on Iran.
The Baltic states have reacted sceptically to Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Vladimir Putin and the US president’s so-called energy ceasefire.
Lithuania’s foreign minister, Keʂtutis Budrys, said Trump’s diesel deal with Vladimir Putin was not helpful. Budrys said:
This deal doesn’t help, neither the crisis of the oil products, nor the unity within the transatlantic community when it concerns Russia. And it is not the European way. Our way is to increase pressure because we already see how it works.
His Estonian counterpart, Margus Tsakhna, gave a similar assessment: “I don’t think that in real life this diesel deal is actually going to change anything on the oil price or diesel price in the market.” He drew a link between US domestic politics and the upcoming midterms.
Estonia’s foreign minister was also sceptical about Trump’s self-proclaimed energy ceasefire. Tsakhna said:
[The] energy ceasefire is not working as President Zelenskyy has said as well. And Russia is really putting more attacks against Ukraine. So what we need to do in Europe, we need to focus on what we can do.
He cited EU sanctions against 1,600 Russian individuals and entities that are due to be signed off later today by the bloc’s 27 foreign ministers, the largest ever-listing of its kind.
Zelenskyy says Ukraine is waiting for the specific details of the “conversation” between the US and Russia after the latest peace talks.
On Friday, negotiators from the US, Ukraine and European countries also held talks in Miami aimed ⁠at ​reaching agreement on a unified peace proposal ​in the coming weeks that could be presented to Russia.
Zelenskyy said in his address that the energy ceasefire could be a “major step” toward ending the war if Trump makes sure Putin honours it.
The Ukrainian leader says Kyiv needs the US to apply real pressure on the Kremlin, not sanction relief or “concessions”.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks to the audience via an online video call during the opening ceremony at the Warsaw Security Forum. Photograph: Omar Marques/Getty Images Zelenskyy said Russia is trying to tactically use the period of cold weather against Ukraine , targeting the country’s power plants and power grids.
“This winter if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,” Zelenskyy said, adding that he supports Trump’s energy ceasefire proposal, but vows that if Russia doesn’t agree to it, then Ukraine “will respond”.
“If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure, and stop killing our people. This is only fair,” Zelenskyy said.
“We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree, if they agree. And we have already shown that we mean it. Last night, Russian oil refineries were not burning but at midnight a Russian jet powered Shahed strike against a production facility in Ukraine.”

However, the deal with Russia was met with backlash from Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who said that it violates U.S. laws.
The telecom sector was also in focus after SpaceX said last week that it had agreed to buy up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band, putting Starlink Mobile on track to compete as a major U.S. mobile carrier.
U.S. stock futures edged higher late Sunday after a drop in oil prices, following U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire" effective immediately.
As of 11:27 p.m. EDT, Dow futures were up about 0.34%, the S&P 500 futures gained 0.31% and the Nasdaq-100 futures climbed 0.43%.

On Friday, the three benchmark indexes closed higher . The Dow Jones Industrial Average led the climb, adding more than 400 points to close up 0.83%. The S&P 500 gained 0.59% at close, while the Nasdaq Composite was up 0.64% at the end of the session.
Last week, all three U.S. benchmark indexes closed higher.
koyfin_20261012_083501091.png Key US Market Drivers
Oil was in focus late Sunday amid the dualities of an energy ceasefire announced between Russia and Ukraine and continued Middle East conflict, which kept prices above $100 a barrel.
Trump announced in a Truth Social post, "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
Earlier on Friday, Trump said that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had agreed to supply diesel to America and the global markets following a discussion. "Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump said.
Oil prices edged lower at the time of writing, although they continued to trade over $100 a barrel. Brent crude futures expiring in December were trading at $102.91 a barrel, down nearly 2%, while WTI crude futures expiring in November traded at $90.03 per barrel.
However, the deal with Russia was met with backlash from Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who said that it violates U.S. laws.
On Sunday, a group of seven senators, including four Republicans and three Democrats, released a statement urging the administration to "immediately reverse course."
"Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine. Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies. President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law," they said.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," they added.
Meanwhile, conflict in the Middle East continued to escalate over the weekend after the Houthis claimed ‌responsibility ⁠for a Saturday strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Additionally, BP withdrew from the World Petroleum Council Energy Congress in Riyadh on Sunday after the attack.
"We made every effort to participate in WPC. ‌Unfortunately, ⁠due to travel disruption, we are unable to be there in person. We greatly value our longstanding partnerships across the region," a BP spokesperson ​reportedly said, as per Reuters.
The telecom sector was also in focus after SpaceX (SPCX) said it had agreed to buy up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band, putting Starlink Mobile on track to compete as a major U.S. mobile carrier.
Shares of other telecom companies including AT&T Inc. (T), T-Mobile US (TMUS), Verizon Inc. (VZ) and Comcast (CMCSA) sank following the announcement.
Meanwhile, investors are gearing up for the third-quarter earnings season, which starts next week with major U.S. banks reporting results.
IREN Ltd. (IREN): Shares of the company jumped 9% in the overnight session late Sunday after a media report indicated that Anthropic is the mystery AI cloud customer that IREN had referenced in its earnings call a few months ago.
WF Holding Limited (WFF): The microcap company drew retail attention after its shares pulled back overnight after jumping more than 499% on Friday amid speculative trading.
Verastem Inc. (VSTM): The biopharmaceutical company was in the spotlight ahead of its investor event on Wednesday, where it is expected to present initial efficacy results and updated safety data for its oral cancer drug.
Cipher Digital Inc. (CIFR): The company's shares moved 2% higher in the overnight session on Sunday, riding in sympathy with peer IREN's steep climb higher.
Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) and the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) all climbed at the time of writing, with sentiment in the 'bullish' territory.

Two more tankers were attacked near the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, one in Hormuz and the other off the coast of Oman, Argus has reported , citing ship-tracking data and the Indian shipping minister.
One of the targets was a Suezmax loaded with Iraqi crude, which had set sail on October 8, the Indian top shipping official said. It was hit by an unknown projectile that caused fire on board and, at the time of writing, two sailors were still missing . The other tanker was a product carrier that was hit by a drone. That attack was reported earlier by the UK Maritime Trade Operations outlet.
"India reiterates the need for immediate de-escalation and a resolution to the ongoing conflict through dialogue and diplomacy," New Delhi's foreign ministry said. "Attacks on commercial vessels, seafarers and civilian infrastructure must cease. Freedom of navigation and the safe, unimpeded flow of maritime commerce through international waterways, in accordance with international law, must be upheld."
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has stepped up attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in the past couple of weeks, targeting vessels trying to transit the strait in dark mode, along a southern corridor near the coast of Oman.
The U.S. Navy is meanwhile striking Iranian-linked vessels, with the strikes heightening the already considerable shipping risk in the area. "All ships within the limits of the Strait of Hormuz that turn off their navigation and identification systems will be identified as hostile and will be dealt with severely and decisively," the IRGC's Navy forces said in a statement, as reported by Iranian state media.
The news of the latest attacks comes alongside a report about a so-called energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, announced by President Trump over the weekend. Neither of the warring parties has confirmed the ceasefire, and Axios has since reported that it is a narrower refinery-only ceasefire proposal, but the news has pressured oil prices. Brent was trading above $103 per barrel after the news, and WTI was over $90 per barrel.

Houthi attack on Riyadh airport forces swift rethink of Trump’s new strategy
US president’s plan to park the wars in Iran and Yemen, while blaming Ukraine for diesel prices, looks unsustainable
The reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also left Donald Trump forced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month.
The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Friday. He said it was the result of “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – which he blamed on Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms.
In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran.
Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea. The fate of Yemen, the poorest country in the world according to the International Monetary Fund, was not going to shift votes in Kansas or Alaska.
Now, after the Riyadh airport attack, it is doubtful, for a basket of reasons, that this anyway threadbare strategy, largely born of desperation, can hold.
For all the talk of the Gulf becoming responsible for its own security, it is doubtful that Saudi Arabia can be left to fend for itself after the carnage in Riyadh. One of the the 12 dead is an American and there may be more among the severely injured. Something is clearly wrong with Saudi defences since the Houthis are firing rockets from 500 miles away, and they are reaching their target too often.
The US has had a unilateral ceasefire with the Houthis since 2025, and once the hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis recommenced in the summer, the pact was quietly renewed. Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Can he spurn them three times? The pressure to act as allies are expected to may prove overwhelming.
But “the blame Zelenskyy, trade with Russia” strategy is anyway unlikely to work. The amount of additional diesel Vladimir Putin will put on the market is not enough to bring down prices at the pump. Russia accounted for about 12% of global diesel shipped by sea. Exports have fallen by about a third, according to calculations by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
The deal has also reawakened Europe’s worst fears about Trump’s relationship with Russia only weeks after Congress had passed a sanctions package against Moscow authorising Trump to penalise buyers of Russian energy.
Europeans know full well that the inflation problem helping to drive populism is caused by the Iran war and not by Zelenskyy’s tactics. The only question is who will say so. The former UK Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson did not hold back, writing: “It is sickening that the USA is now lifting sanctions on Russian fuel, and transparently ridiculous to blame Ukraine for the spike in prices that obviously began with the closure of the strait of Hormuz. Putin is murdering innocent Ukrainian civilians every day. The Ukrainians are fighting for their lives. And yet the White House is apparently determined to force American drivers to bankroll Putin’s slaughter.”
The German education minister and a member of the CDU, Karin Prien, said: “For a few litres of diesel. What moral bankruptcy.”
Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general and Trump ally, will this week travel to Estonia, one of the countries most supportive of Ukraine. He will have some explaining to do. Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, vowed that EU foreign ministers on Monday will impose the biggest package of sanctions in its history, and he, along with Sweden, now wants to revisit using frozen Russian assets to help Ukraine.
What is worse, it looks as if the political damage to the Republicans caused by the Iran war is irrecoverable. Polls show the ship has sailed. The war has already been weaponised as a pocketbook issue by every Democratic candidate in every TV debate. Republican candidates, challenged to disown the war, are scrambling for the relative safety of identity politics.
The Iranians are also trying to maximise the damage they cause in the strait of Hormuz, countering the Trump narrative that the blockade has been broken. Scenes of tankers on fire are proliferating.
So Trump post-Riyadh needs to rethink. He can rejoin the war against the Houthis, ending the unilateral US ceasefire, but, if so, he knows from experience this will be costly. The first three weeks of the war against Iran cost $1bn a day. Many of the US president’s advisers say he may as well also attack Iran, the Houthis’ backers, as Tehran expects him to do. The Iranian military nevertheless still believes it has escalation dominance, and what happened in Riyadh can be repeated across the Gulf.
The alternative is that his team can negotiate discreetly and indirectly with Tehran as is occurring in Doha. Some Iranians are urging their leadership to seize the chance, arguing Trump is uniquely vulnerable in the run-up to the midterms.
A deal could be done, including on uranium enrichment, but it would not be palatable for the US – or for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election chances.
China and Russia are trying to sort out the Houthis diplomatically, but the Houthi objectives are broadening, while the south of Yemen is split about its future inside the country, a division that harms the country’s ability to be the ground component that Saudi Arabia needs to supplement its air-power dominance. Taiz, the third city of Yemen, is struggling to overcome a Houthi siege. The Saudis can deliver retribution, but retribution is not a solution to a decade-long civil war.
So for the moment the twin Trump strategy – to park the Iran and Yemen conflicts while blaming Zelenskyy – is now so transparent, so morally craven, and in its own terms so ineffective, that it looks unsustainable. The only question is whether the strategy will be jettisoned by the president or instead just rejected by the American people at the ballot box.

items.summary: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the FOMC Just Fired a Warning Shot at the Second-Priciest Stock Market in History  The Motl
items.content:
This has been a year highlighted by a changing of the guard. Longtime CEOs Warren Buffett and Tim Cook handed over the keys to their respective successors, and President Donald Trump's Fed chair nominee, Kevin Warsh, became only the 17th head of the central bank on May 22.
Despite these changes, Wall Street's preeminent stock indexes, the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI +0.83% ) , S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.59% ) , and Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC +0.64% ) have been unstoppable. The artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out and otherworldly growth prospects accompanying this game-changing innovation have lifted the broader market to new heights.
This won't be a one-and-done rate-hiking cycle. Image source: Official Federal Reserve Photo.
But sustaining this AI-driven bull market could be easier said than done. Last week, Fed Chair Warsh and his Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) colleagues fired an unmistakable warning shot at the second-priciest stock market in history. The only question is: How many investors are paying attention?
The Federal Reserve's rate-hiking cycle is ramping up
On Sept. 16, Warsh and 11 other voting members of the FOMC unanimously raised the federal funds target rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00%. It's just the fourth time this century that the central bank has kicked off a rate-hiking cycle .
Warsh and the FOMC have been compelled to act because of persistently elevated inflation. August marked the 66th consecutive month in which the annualized inflation rate topped the FOMC's long-term 2% target.
"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," https://t.co/htRQqyQHtr
While rising prices are perfectly normal in an expanding economy, inflation has soared in 2026 due to Trumpflation (inflation that's specifically driven by President Trump's policies). Donald Trump's tariffs are increasing domestic manufacturing costs, while the Iran war has led to the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The largest energy supply disruption in modern history has sent fuel prices soaring.
The newly released Federal Reserve meeting minutes (effectively a summary of what policymakers discussed behind closed doors on Sept. 15-16) point to tariffs, the Iran war, and the AI infrastructure build-out as key sources of inflation.
More importantly, the Fed meeting minutes charted a path forward for interest rates. Contained in the Fed minutes was this statement:
With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond this current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end. While this statement doesn't tell us whether the FOMC would raise interest rates at the October or December meeting, it makes it crystal clear that additional rate hikes are expected in the not-too-distant future. That's terrible news for a historically expensive stock market.
Stock Market Shiller PE Ratio on the verge of taking out its Dot Com Bubble all-time high 🚨 🤯 👀 https://t.co/CtCmSgWnLt
A truly jaw-dropping amount of capital is being spent on the AI data center build-out , part of which has been financed with debt. If lending costs rise, as the FOMC's September meeting minutes imply, it could slow this expansion and adversely impact lofty growth expectations.
In June, the S&P 500's Shiller Price-to-Earnings Ratio came within a stone's throw of surpassing the priciest valuation multiple in 156 years , achieved just before the dot-com bubble burst. This is a stock market with little to no margin for error. If the Fed's rate-hiking cycle ramps up, maintaining this aggressive AI build-out without any "hiccups" would likely prove impossible.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy says oil tanker struck mine in Strait of Hormuz
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy says oil tanker struck mine in Strait of Hormuz
IRGC Navy says explosion struck engine room of supertanker capable of carrying 2 million barrels of oil
ISTANBUL An oil tanker struck a mine while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz, triggering an explosion in its engine room, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said Sunday.
The IRGC Navy said in a statement that the supertanker, capable of carrying around 2 million barrels of oil, was attempting to transit the strategic waterway with its navigation system switched off.
The oil tanker is the third vessel to strike naval mines along the prohibited route in the Strait of Hormuz since Saturday, it added.
The statement did not identify the vessel or specify its nationality or flag.
The IRGC Navy renewed its warning that vessels switching off their navigation systems while passing through the waterway would be classified as “hostile vessels.”
The announcement came after the US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in late August that international shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz had been reopened following the removal of Iranian naval mines by US forces.
Iran announced on July 12 that it had again closed the strait following the resumption of US attacks on July 8.
Tehran has threatened to target vessels using routes other than those designated by Iranian authorities or attempting to cross the waterway without permission.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, while Washington later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The US and Iran subsequently signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the strait, but implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway.

items.title: Ukraine strikes Yandex data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
items.summary: It is the third time this week that Ukraine has targeted Russian tech giant Yandex, forcing the company to suspend its operations.
items.content:
Image caption, Yandex's data centres have been targeted three times this week - like this one in Sasovo on Thursday
Yandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on the Russian tech giant's sites this week.
The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users.
Earlier this week, Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its services after two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues in its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion.
Kyiv said it was targeting places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex.
Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market - a deal that has drawn criticism from Europe and sparked a diplomatic row with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity.
The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices.
The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.
On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed.
Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad.

Share Netanyahu demands probe into sources for award-winning Gaza film NAZA on social media
A man walks past an image of directors Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, winners of the special jury prize at the Venice International Film Festival for their film NAZA, with the Hebrew word for "traitors" scrawled across in graffiti, in Ashdod, Israel, on September 15, 2026 [Ariel Schalit/AP]
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has called for an investigation into the anonymous sources featured in a documentary alleging that Israel’s military killed civilians in Gaza using AI-powered targeting systems.
The award-winning film, NAZA, draws on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers accusing the army of using the systems to kill numerous civilians in the besieged territory.

“I demand that the chief of general staff, the head of the Shin Bet, and the attorney general launch a comprehensive investigation into the participants in the film ‘Naza’ and prosecute them for serious information security violations, criminal libel, and harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests,” Netanyahu said on X on Saturday evening.
“The film presents a false, misleading, and biased narrative that defames the State of Israel and the [Israeli military] internationally, severely damaging Israel’s standing,” he added.
In a statement last month, the Israeli military said it “categorically” rejected the whistleblowers’ allegations, calling some of their assertions “absurd’ and contradictory.
It insisted that the selection and approval of strikes “are made by human personnel only”, in line with the military’s guidelines.
Israeli army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir has called for legal action against the participants to be considered and ordered an investigation into suspected leaks of classified military information used in the film’s production.
NAZA takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in air strikes, an abbreviated form of the Hebrew phrase for “collateral damage”.
The film was awarded a special jury prize at the Venice International Film Festival and received a historic 25-minute standing ovation.
The film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, have been accused of “treason”. Netanyahu and Culture Minister Miki Zohar have threatened to revoke their Israeli citizenship.
Last week, the head of Israel’s National Public Diplomacy Directorate, Tzipi Hotovely, awarded the creators of another film, NAZA: The Real Story, certificates of recognition for countering the “blood libels” made in the original NAZA film.
According to a statement from the Prime Minister’s Office, NAZA: The Real Story features testimony from soldiers refuting the original claims.
In contrast, 43 Israeli rights groups defended the filmmakers of NAZA and denounced the threats being directed at them, according to Israel’s Channel 12 news.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began on October 7, 2023, after Hamas’s armed wing, the Qassam Brigades, and other Palestinian groups attacked southern Israel, killing 1,139 people and taking about 240 captive.
Since then, Israel has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

items.title: India’s retail inflation jumps to 5.54% in September, above estimates
items.summary: India inflations jumps for the 11-straight month, raising prospects of a further interest rate hike
items.content:
India’s retail inflation jumps to 5.54% in September, above estimates
India’s consumer price inflation increased to 5.54% in September from 4.82% in August.
India's central bank expects core inflation to be at 4.4% for the financial year ending March 2027 and headline inflation at 5.2%, higher than its medium-term target of 4%.
Shoppers gather at New Market in Kolkata, India, on September 21, 2026, ahead of the Durga Puja festival.
India's headline inflation rose to 5.54% in September from 4.82% in August , adding pressure on the country's central bank to further tighten monetary policy.
The consumer price index print was slightly above economists' expectations of 5.40%, according to a Reuters poll. Inflation has been on the rise for 11 straight months in the world's fastest-growing economy and has touched a 22-month high in September.
India's food inflation climbed 7.74% in September from 5.97% the month prior, with prices rising faster in rural areas than cities, India's Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation said in a Monday release. Transport services for goods inflation rose 14.73% while that for personal transport jumped 7.46%, as per the release.
Earlier this month, the Reserve Bank of India raised its interest rates for the first time since 2023 , joining several major central banks in tightening monetary policy in a bid to arrest accelerating inflation. India's central bank also said that in the "current conditions" further rate cuts were "off the table in the near term" and policy action could either be a rate hike or a pause.
India is among the countries most  vulnerable to the supply disruptions  caused by the Iran war. It imports nearly 85% of its fuel needs, and before the Iran war it heavily relied on energy supplies through the  Strait of Hormuz .
Oil prices have been elevated due to the tensions in the Middle East. Experts, however, predict that prices will remain volatile in the near term amid concerns over the Middle East conflict and the impact of Hurricane Isaias.
India's central bank expects core inflation to be at 4.4% for the financial year ending March 2027 and headline inflation at 5.2%, which is higher than the RBI's medium-term target of 4%.
The RBI raised India's economic growth estimate by 40 basis points to 7.1% but cautioned that protracted geopolitical tensions, trade frictions, tightening of financial conditions and elevated international commodity prices would likely weigh on economic activity.
Food prices in particular and India's rural economy also face an added risk from the Super El Nino , with the country receiving its lowest rainfall in over a decade during June to September, a key season for its largely rain-fed farms and reservoirs.
The rainfall was the fourth lowest since 2001, and the 13th driest since 1901, according to the India Meteorological Department. Several parts of key farm states such as Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, and Haryana are facing extreme drought conditions.
HSBC said in a report on Oct. 7 that it expects another rate hike in December, a day after the RBI policy action. "This may not be a deep tightening cycle, but a tightening cycle it is," the analysts said, adding that the September retail inflation data is likely to show a "sizeable headline pop."

Fighting also continues near the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military announced Sunday that it had disabled a cargo vessel after the crew "ignored warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade" of Iran's ports and vessels.
Iran says U.S. and Israel responsible for Strait of Hormuz disruption
Iranian Foreign Minister Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei blamed the U.S. and Israel on Monday for the ongoing disruption to commercial shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
During his weekly press briefing, Baghaei noted that before the U.S. and Israel launched joint airstrikes on Iran at the end of February, the Strait of Hormuz was open.
"Everything we are witnessing in the region" was a result of the "actions of the United States and the Israeli regime," including the economic consequences of the disruption to shipping through the strait, Baghaei said.
"If the governments that are concerned about this situation are genuinely serious about their concerns, they should address the party responsible for creating this situation and seize every opportunity to compel the United States to stop its acts of aggression," he said.
Tehran and Washington both claim to have control over the strait, and they are imposing competing blockades in the Persian Gulf and the strait.
President Trump has offered various justifications for launching the war on Iran, but has recently stressed it as a necessary means of ensuring the regime in Tehran cannot build a nuclear weapon.

Houthi fighters have ramped up their siege of the Yemeni city of Taiz, where fighting has killed more than 60 people in the past 24 hours, military sources from both sides told the French news agency AFP on Monday.
The Houthis have blocked all exits from the city - a major urban center in Yemen's southwest that, if it falls to the Iranian proxy force would give the Houthis a strategic foothold from which to threaten the de facto Yemeni government capital of Aden, further to the south.
The fighting over the last day alone has killed at least 22 pro-government forces and 40 Houthi fighters, the sources said. The Houthi sources told AFP reinforcements were being sent to the area.
On Sunday, health officials warned of a "humanitarian catastrophe" in Taiz, with medicine, medical equipment and fuel "on the verge of running out."
Taiz is inland from the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where the Houthis captured swathes of territory in a rapid offensive last month.

Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Friday that he'd struck a deal to buy diesel during a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, aiming to tamp down a spike in fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections.
But the plan runs counter to U.S. efforts to cut the flow of money Russia gets from oil and gas sales that can be used to pay for its war against Ukraine . A bipartisan group of six U.S. senators called Sunday for the administration to "immediately reverse course" on the plan.

Airstrikes targeted two districts in Yemen's Houthi-held capital of Sanaa, the Iran-backed rebel group said Monday, accusing Saudi Arabia of launching the attacks around midnight local time.
A spokesman for Yemen's Houthi-run health ministry said the strikes killed one person and wounded 12 others in Sanaa.
Ministry spokesman Anees al-Asbahi said a strike on a salt factory in Sanaa's Hamadan district killed on eman and wounded eight people. A separate strike on a house wounded a woman and three children, he said.

Those attacks have killed at least 20 people at Saudi airports over the last week, including three killed on Oct. 6 and 7 at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport; three killed at King Khalid on Oct. 8; 13 people killed by the deadliest single strike on Riyadh's airport Saturday; and one who died in the latest attack on the facility on Sunday.

"I can tell you that the exchange of messages between Iran and the United States through mediators is continuing," Baghaei said, adding that there had "already been considerable discussion of the seven points" in the proposal.

Balkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for Greece
Clear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean Sea
Temperatures fluctuated dramatically in the Balkans last week, with unusually large differences between daytime highs and overnight lows – known as the diurnal range.
An area of high pressure over the region brought prolonged sunshine during the day, while clear skies at night allowed temperatures to drop rapidly as heat escaped into the atmosphere without cloud cover to slow the cooling.
In Kosanica, Montenegro , the average maximum temperature in October is 15C (59F), while the average minimum is 4C. However, on 4 and 5 October the difference between daytime highs and overnight lows reached 30C, more than double the October average.
Elsewhere in Europe , high pressure will build across the north and west over the coming week, pushing an area of low pressure southwards towards the Mediterranean. The low-pressure system will deepen as it crosses the Adriatic and Ionian seas before moving eastwards into the Aegean Sea by the middle of the week.
Spells of heavy rain and strong winds are expected to sweep across Greece as a result. Forecast models suggest widespread rainfall of 50-150mm, with the highest totals expected around the island of Skiathos.
Towards the end of the week, the system will continue eastwards, bringing showers to parts of Crete, which was hit by severe flooding a week earlier. Those storms swept some cars and trees into the sea.
People cross a bridge over a swollen river as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico’s Pacific coast in Costalegre, Jalisco state. Photograph: Daniel Becerril/Reuters Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon, a category 4 storm, is moving close to Mexico’s Pacific coast, near the state of Jalisco. It is the latest of 21 named storms in the Pacific this season, 11 of which have reached hurricane strength.
At the time of writing, Simon has a central pressure of 933mb and maximum sustained winds of nearly 150mph (241km/h). However, the hurricane is expected to weaken rapidly if its core moves onshore, cutting it off from the warm ocean waters that fuel it.
Heavy rainfall is affecting south-western Mexico, where totals could reach 300-400mm across a wide area, rising to 400-500mm in the wettest locations.

Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week.
The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries.
Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs . Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”.
Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket
The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.
Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China .
On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.
Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints.
“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said.
Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too.
The new all-electric ID Tiguan. Photograph: Volkswagen AG Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.”
Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin.
Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”.
The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes.
On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.

Oil prices reversed initial losses early Monday, despite the potential for improved supplies after U.S. President Donald Trump declared an " energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery rose 0.92% $105.68 a barrel. U.S.  West Texas Intermediate futures  for November ticked 0.95% higher to $92.72 per barrel. Prices on both benchmarks had fallen by around 1.5% earlier in the session.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump said in a social media statement Sunday stateside.
Oil reversed its losses after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed such a ceasefire, but warned Monday that Moscow must do the same.
Prospects of more Russian energy hitting markets after a deal with the U.S. have also risen after Trump said Friday that Moscow will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under a deal he struck with Putin during a phone call.
Elsewhere early on Monday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said it was dealing with another round of drones and missiles attacks directed at Saudi Arabia.
It comes after Iran's Minister of Foreign Affairs Abbas Araghchi made a phone call to Saudi Arabia's Minister of Foreign Affairs Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah to discuss the region's recent escalation of events as well as the efforts to address it, according to the Saudi state news agency ,

The Dow Jones , S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 have held steady in recent weeks as investors have focused on rising US bond yields and the escalating situation in the Middle East. Their resilience will be tested in the coming weeks as major US companies report earnings and key economic data is released.
Dow Jones, S&P 500, and Nasdaq 100 to React to Earnings Season
The main catalyst for the US stock market this week will be the upcoming earnings season , which will kick off on Tuesday. Top US banks, including popular names like Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan, will release their numbers. Other non-bank companies that will release their numbers are Johnson & Johnson, UnitedHealth Group and Kinder Morgan.
Analysts are optimistic about this earnings season. FactSet (NYSE: FDS ) data shows that the estimate among analysts is that earnings growth will be 29.5%. Historically, the real earnings growth tends to be 7% above the estimate. As such, there is a likelihood that the growth will be over 40%.

These numbers will provide more hints about what to expect from the Federal Reserve. Economists expect the bank to leave rates unchanged in this meeting and then hike in December.
The stock market will also react to the bond market , where the ten-year and five-year yields have pulled back in the past few days.
The US stock market will also react to the ongoing crisis in the Middle East, which is escalating. For example, Yemen’s Houthis launched a major attack against Saudi Arabia’s main airport, with President Donald Trump hinting that the US will intervene .
Iran has also continued striking ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz. There is also fear that the crisis will escalate. S&P 500’s Narrow Rally Faces Fresh Tests From CPI, Bank Earnings: 3 Charts To Watch This Week
The S&P 500 has climbed roughly 80% since the start of 2024, but the equal-weight index has lagged as gains concentrate in the largest companies.
Traders work before the closing bell at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) (Photo credit should read JOHANNES EISELE/AFP via Getty Images)
The VIX-to-three-month volatility ratio is near the low end of its two-year range, suggesting investors are paying relatively little for near-term protection.
Regional banks are underperforming the broader market, putting loan quality, funding costs and net interest income in focus as earnings season begins.
Wednesday's September CPI report could shift expectations for the Federal Reserve's next move and test the market's confidence.
The stock market looks calm, but three charts suggest a more complicated picture. The S&P 500 is near record highs even as its rally remains concentrated, options markets show limited demand for near-term protection, and regional banks continue to lag. September inflation data and a fresh round of bank earnings could test that uneasy balance this week.
The S&P 500 has climbed roughly 80% since the start of 2024, but gains have not been evenly distributed across the market. The market-cap-weighted index has outpaced its equal-weight counterpart by about 16 percentage points, underscoring how much the rally has depended on a smaller group of large-cap stocks.
SPX vs. RSP/SPY charted year-to-date. | Source: Koyfin The rally has also narrowed since the spring 2026 low. Concentration is not a sell signal, but it changes the risk. An index held up by a few names is more exposed to a single earnings miss or a jump in yields.
Strong inflation data this week could complicate the outlook for rate cuts and weigh on risk appetite, while a softer reading could help support stocks beyond the market’s biggest names.
The  SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) traded flat in pre-market trade on Monday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the ETF trended in ‘bullish’ territory over the past day.
Options Markets Show Little Demand For Near-Term Protection
The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) is often called Wall Street’s fear gauge. It measures how much investors are paying for insurance against near-term swings in the S&P 500. This chart compares that short-term price with the price of insurance three months out. Right now short-term protection is cheaper, which is what you’d expect when nobody is worried about the next few weeks.
VIX/VIX3M vs. SPX charted year-to-date. | Source: Koyfin A reading below 1 suggests traders are pricing in less near-term volatility than volatility over a longer horizon. The ratio is near the low end of its two-year range.
The spikes above 1.0 are sharp and short-lived. They came in August 2024, December 2024 and April 2025, the last of which peaked near 1.28. In each case, the move came fast and with little warning.
That calm could hold if economic data and corporate results reassure investors. However, a hotter inflation reading or an earnings surprise could quickly change the picture, making the reaction in volatility markets worth watching.
Big banks have not moved as a group this year.  Citigroup (C) is up 11.1% and  Morgan Stanley (MS) is up 7.0%.  JPMorgan (JPM) is up 3.3% and  Goldman Sachs (GS) is up 1.9%.  Bank of America (BAC) is down 1.2%, and  Wells Fargo (WFC) is down 10.4%. That is a spread of more than 20 points between the best and worst names.
Big banks and KRE/SPY year-to-date. | Source: Koyfin Meanwhile,  the regional bank ETF relative to the S&P 500 is at 0.0886, its lowest level of the year. Higher-for-longer rates can help margins, but they can also raise funding costs and credit worries, and regionals tend to feel that first.
The  Financial Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLF) edged up as much as 0.3% in pre-market trading. Retail sentiment around the ETF trended in ‘bullish’ territory over the past day.
Earnings reports could offer a clearer view of those pressures, particularly through net interest income, deposit costs and loan-loss provisions. The results may help determine whether regional banks’ underperformance reflects lingering sector-specific concerns or a broader risk to financial stocks.
A hot inflation report: If inflation comes in above forecasts, expect talk of another Fed hike in October to come roaring back. One outlook noted that a rise in services prices to its highest level since July 2022 means a hot reading would put an October hike back in play. That would hit a narrow market with low insurance coverage, which is the combination we’ve described across the charts.
An in-line report:  If inflation matches expectations, the market probably breathes out. That keeps the focus on earnings and gives the record highs a chance to hold.
A cool report:  If inflation comes in below forecasts, hike fears should fade. The more interesting question is who benefits. If the rally broadens beyond the largest companies, the first chart will start to heal.

Australia, New Zealand, the U.K., the U.S., France, Germany, Japan and others have warned against travel to the kingdom, which is hosting the World ⁠Petroleum Congress.

Saudi Arabia said Monday it was dealing with more drones and missile strikes as a slew of countries warned against travel to the kingdom due to fatal attacks on Riyadh airport by Iran-backed Houthi  militants.
The Australian and New Zealand governments on Monday cautioned their citizens against traveling to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and other Saudi destinations, joining similar advisories from the U.K., U.S., Canada, France, Germany, Japan and others.
It came as the Saudi aviation authority extended the suspension of operations at the airport, which has been hit by numerous projectiles over the last week. The deadliest strike came on Saturday, when 12 people were killed and more than 300 were injured, according to officials . Another strike on Sunday killed one person and injured nearly a dozen.
Who are the Houthis? U.S. and U.K. strikes thrust Iran-backed group into the global spotlight

The fatalities come as the kingdom hosts major corporate conferences, including the World ⁠Petroleum Congress, the International Energy Forum Ministerial Meeting and the Future Investment Initiative.
Surveillance footage shows smoke and fire at the moment of an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 10, 2026, in this frame from a handout video.

items.content:
Follow updates on the war in the Middle East for Monday, October 12, here . See earlier developments below.
There was another strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, after an attack the previous day killed at least 12 people and wounded another 309, according to Saudi authorities. An American was among those victims. The Iran-backed Houthis have claimed responsibility for the strikes.
President Trump on Saturday left open the possibility the U.S. will join Saudi Arabia's battle against the Houthis. "We may. We're gonna look at it," Mr. Trump said. Fighting between the Iranian proxy group and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen appears to be the new epicenter of the wider war .
President Trump spoke with Russian leader Vladimir Putin on Friday to discuss freeing up millions of tons of diesel , but the Russian president also relayed Iran's position on a peace deal to his American counterpart, according to the Kremlin.
Saudi authorities say King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was attacked
Saudi's General Authority of Civil Aviation on Sunday confirmed that King Fahd International Airport had been attacked after the Iran-backed Houthis said they had targeted the airport in Dammam.
It's unclear whether there were any injuries. The Saudi civil aviation authority said it is assessing the damage .
King Fahd International Airport is located approximately 400 miles away from the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which was also attacked on Sunday.
https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-elections-saudi-arabia-yemen-houthis/#post-update-070a5f14
Saudi, Egypt, Pakistan and Turkey condemn Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Pakistan and Turkey on Sunday issued a joint statement condemning the Houthis' attacks against Saudi Arabia, including the latest strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport.
The regional group of four nations said the attacks in Riyadh, which killed at least 12 people and wounded another 309 the previous day, "constitute a blatant violation of international law."
An American was among those victims. Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said those killed also included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis and one person each from Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan.
https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-elections-saudi-arabia-yemen-houthis/#post-update-705b8589
Iran calls U.S. response "insufficient" amid stalled talks to end the war
The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said Tehran considers the latest U.S. response "insufficient," amid stalled negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz.
The comments by Mohsen Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander, were reported by Iran's state-run IRNA news agency.
Rezaei added that Iran is no longer responding to the U.S. and said Washington must clarify certain issues, without giving details. He said the U.S. has accepted some of the seven conditions but others remain unclear.
Iran's delegation to the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders last month proposed a sped-up agreement that echoed the memorandum of understanding that collapsed days after the U.S. and Iran signed it in June. The new proposal was rejected, but the two sides have remained in contact via mediation.
Rezaei also threatened "cables, data centers, AI facilities and other sites in the region" if intense fighting breaks out again.
https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-elections-saudi-arabia-yemen-houthis/#post-update-ac11baa4
Houthis claim Saudi airport attacks, including new strike on Sunday
Another projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. The latest attack came one day after a missile hit the same airport terminal, killing 12 people and injuring hundreds.
Details about the latest strike on the King Khalid International Airport complex weren't immediately available, outside of the fact that terminals 3 and 4, for domestic flights, were affected. The missile attack Saturday was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Of around 300 people wounded in its aftermath, some suffered critical injuries. The airport was closed Sunday.
The newest attack happened as the Houthis said they carried out at least four operations targeting the airport in Riyadh since Saturday. Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on Telegram that the attacks came in response to "brutal Saudi aggression against our country and our people," CBS News partner BBC News reported . He claimed Saudi Arabia launched more than 120 airstrikes in the past 24 hours in parts of Yemen under Houthi control.
https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-elections-saudi-arabia-yemen-houthis/#post-update-39e81e9f
Sen. Chris Murphy warns against U.S. retaliating on Saudi's behalf amid war "spiraling out of control"
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy, of Connecticut, said the U.S. shouldn't retaliate on Saudi Arabia's behalf following the strike at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, arguing that going to war with the Houthis in Yemen would be an escalation with dangerous consequences.
"This administration is absolutely incompetent in war-making, and so just as we have made the Middle East worse and more chaotic by getting involved in a war against Iran, we would simply escalate and make the situation even more dangerous," Murphy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
Murphy, who said he was at the Riyadh airport the day before the strike, said, "What I saw on the ground is a war that is spiraling out of control."
Murphy cited the 12 people killed in the airport strike, a "full-blown new war" between the Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, the Iranians restarting their missile programs, and evidence that he said suggests they're restarting nuclear research activities, along with the deaths of American service members and the war's high price tag.
"If the Trump administration was trying to lose this war, they couldn't do worse than they are doing," Murphy said. "This is a humiliation to the United States. The war is getting bigger and more dangerous, not smaller and more limited."
https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-elections-saudi-arabia-yemen-houthis/#post-update-5cb4be7d
Netanyahu denounces Riyadh attack, calls for a region "united against threats"
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke out Sunday in the wake of the deadly attack on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport, joining leaders from other countries in the region and beyond who've condemned it. The U.S., Israel and other nations have blamed Yemen's Houthis for the strike, although the group hasn't claimed responsibility for it outright.
"Terrorism targets innocent people and seeks to spread fear and instability. It must be confronted with resolve," said Netanyahu in a statement posted to X . "Israel looks forward to a strong Middle East—one that stands united against threats, protects its people, and builds a future of security, cooperation, and prosperity for all the peoples of our region."
Netanyahu also shared "condolences to the families of those murdered" and "wishes for a full recovery to the injured."
https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-elections-saudi-arabia-yemen-houthis/#post-update-2888e4d1
